title: ‘Ah Girl’ Wins Best Film at Singapore’s Silver Screen Awards as Shahrbanoo Sadat Takes Director Prize
full_text: × Oct 31, 2026 8:00am PT ‘Ah Girl’ Wins Best Film at Singapore’s Silver Screen Awards as Shahrbanoo Sadat Takes Director Prize By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59 5 hours ago Sourav Ganguly’s ‘Bigg Boss Bangla’ Among Highlights as Indian Media Giant JioStar Revenues Climb 10% 9 hours ago How Keanu Reeves Landed in Stop-Motion Samurai Epic ‘Hidari’ – and Why S.S. Rajamouli Wanted to Know How It Was Made 10 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ah Girl' Courtesy of the Toronto Film Festival Singaporean filmmaker Ang Geck Geck Priscilla’s debut feature “ Ah Girl ” won best film in the Asian Feature Film Competition at the Singapore International Film Festival ’s Silver Screen Awards on Saturday. The film follows a seven-year-old girl in 1990s Singapore whose parents have separated. Ang workshopped the project at the festival’s Southeast Asian Film Lab back in 2015, and “Ah Girl” went on to take the Youth Jury Award at the International Film Festival Rotterdam. Ang is an alumna of the Busan Asian Film Academy. Her 2012 short “Broken Crayon” won the Singapore Short Film Awards’ best short film prize. Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat won best director for “No Good Men,” which opened the Berlinale. Set in Kabul just before the Taliban come back to power, the drama follows a camerawoman whose work, family and freedom are suddenly in doubt. Sadat, who has lived in Germany since 2021, made the 2016 Cannes premiere “Wolf and Sheep” and 2019’s “The Orphanage.” The jury split the best performance prize. Pushpa Thing Lama was honored for “Elephants in the Fog,” about a member of Nepal’s third-gender Kinnar community searching for her missing daughter. Putri Marino shared the award for “Four Seasons in Java,” a magical realist drama about a woman who goes back to her hometown after two decades behind bars. The Special Jury Prize went to Japanese director Nagahisa Makoto’s “Burn,” his second feature, which premiered at Sundance. Nagahisa won awards at the same festival for his short “And So We Put Goldfish in the Pool” (2017) and his feature “We Are Little Zombies” (2019). In the Southeast Asian Short Film Competition, Yogyakarta-based artist-filmmaker Arief Budiman’s “Golden Island” was named best Southeast Asian short. The film, which competed at Rotterdam, follows a videographer from Java and another from Papua as they make a film about Papua together. Thai director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke won best director for “The Bovine Comedy,” a Locarno premiere set in a 2036 where cows have nearly died out. His feature debut “A Useful Ghost” (2025) won the Critics’ Week Grand Prize at Cannes and received a special mention at SGIFF. German-Indonesian filmmaker Berthold Wahjudi took the shorts Special Jury Prize for “‘Vaterland’ or A Bule Named Yanto,” which premiered in Cannes’ Critics’ Week. Sarah Lingam won best performance for “Flame of the Forest,” about a young nurse who returns home and is blamed for her grandmother’s death. Singaporean experimental animator Exyl’s “Singapore God” was named best Singapore short. The Audience Choice Award went to Singapore Panorama Programme 2, “Second Life, Second Skin,” a package of five shorts: Shara Tay’s “Kiss Me Climax,” Ash Goh Hua’s “Subterranea,” Syahmi Iman’s “Reanimator,” Leon Cheo’s “Orang Minyak” and Ewan Leong’s “Encik.” Prizes were also handed out at the SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum, held Oct. 30. “Agape,” from Yamaguchi Shin and Miyahara Takuya, won the SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award. The SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award (Asian Producers Network) went to Lệ Diễm Hà’s “Dear Son An.” Tong Khoon Mun and Zhou Ke Xin’s “Beg, Borrow, Steal” won the SGIFF Abroad Award supported by Sony, and Sam Chua Weishi and Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal” received the SGIFF Abroad Award. Earlier in the festival, Indian star Aamir Khan received the SGIFF Screen Icon Award from Peter Chan during an In Conversation With session on Oct. 22. Kore-eda Hirokazu, who released two features this year, “Sheep in the Box” and “Look Back,” was presented with the SGIFF Cinema Honorary Award by Boo Junfeng on Oct. 24. The ceremony took place at the Singtel Waterfront Theatre on the penultimate day of the 37th SGIFF, which runs through Nov. 1. Launched in 1991, the Silver Screen Awards was the first international film competition to include a dedicated section for Asian cinema. The full list of winners: ASIAN FEATURE FILM COMPETITION Best Film: “Ah Girl” – Ang Geck Geck Best Director: Shahrbanoo Sadat – “No Good Men” Best Performance: Pushpa Thing Lama – “Elephants in the Fog”; Putri Marino – “Four Seasons in Java” Special Jury Prize: “Burn” – Nagahisa Makoto SOUTHEAST ASIAN SHORT FILM COMPETITION Best Southeast Asian Short Film: “Golden Island” – Arief Budiman Best Director: Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke – “The Bovine Comedy” Special Jury Prize: “‘Vaterland’ or A Bule Named Yanto” – Berthold Wahjudi Best Performance: Sarah Lingam – “Flame of the Forest” Best Singapore Short Film: “Singapore God” – Exyl AUDIENCE CHOICE AWARD Singapore Panorama Program 2: “Second Life, Second Skin” – “Kiss Me Climax” (Shara Tay), “Subterranea” (Ash Goh Hua), “Reanimator” (Syahmi Iman), “Orang Minyak” (Leon Cheo), “Encik” (Ewan Leong) SGIFF PRO PITCHING FORUM AWARDS SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award: “Agape” – Yamaguchi Shin, Miyahara Takuya SGIFF Pro Pitching Forum Award (Asian Producers Network): “Dear Son An” – Lệ Diễm Hà SGIFF Abroad Award supported by Sony: “Beg, Borrow, Steal” – Tong Khoon Mun, Zhou Ke Xin SGIFF Abroad Award: “Primal” – Sam Chua Weishi, Rein Maychaelson SPECIAL RECOGNITION AWARDS SGIFF Screen Icon Award: Aamir Khan SGIFF Cinema Honorary Award: Kore-eda Hirokazu France Riots Put Hollywood Shoots on Alert as Curfews Disrupt Movie Theaters: It ‘Has Now Been Flagged as a Problem Area’ Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations Blackpink and ‘White Lotus’ Star Lisa Documentary ‘Always Lalisa’ Sets Global Release Alexander Ludwig on ‘Unabomber’ Movie, His ‘Hunger Games’ Death Scene and ‘White Lotus’ Season 4: ‘It’s F—ing Wild’ Loading comments...

title: Emmy-Winning Comedian Alex Edelman Says Loss Of Kennedy Center Is No Joke
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Daytime Emmy Winners: ‘General Hospital’ Wins Sixth Best Drama Series In A Row; ‘Kelly Clarkson’ Takes Talk Series Trophy In Final Year Read the full story By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg John “Bobby” Wright Dies: ‘McHale’s Navy’ Actor, Singer & Son Of Country Icon Kitty Wells Was 84 Tony-Winning Broadway Director Daniel Sullivan Announces Retirement After 55-Year Career; Jonathan Kent Steps In For Upcoming ‘Montauk’ ‘A Few Good Men’ Broadway Review: Bradley Whitford And Tom Blyth Manhandle The Truth View All October 31, 2026 7:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alex Edelman wins at the Emmys Kevin Winter/Getty Images Alex Edelman , the comedian and actor who won an Emmy for his 2024 HBO/Max special Just For Us and a special Tony for the original Broadway staging, laments what is effectively the loss to comics of a newly politicized Kennedy Center . “For me and the performers I know, it doesn’t make sense to play the venue now unless you’re avowedly and solidly Trump-supporting,” Edelman, who currently writes and stars in Peacock’s The Paper , says in a guest column for The New York Times . “By my count, only three headlining comedians performed at the Kennedy Center this year, all vocal Trump supporters at some point.” Related Stories News Kennedy Center Honors To Move To D.C.'s Capital One Arena Amid Closure Of Arts Complex News Barbra Streisand Decries Trump's "Unchecked Ego" Amid His Assertion That The Kennedy Center May Be Torn Down Fondly recalling his 2024 performance of his one-man show Just Like Us at the Kennedy Center’s Eisenhower Theater – “My parents came down from Boston for it” – Edelman writes, “That might have been my last time performing there.” Watch on Deadline As Deadline’s Ted Johnson noted earlier this month , the fall-out from President Donald Trump’s takeover of the arts institution in 2025 is ongoing. One of the latest developments was the news this month that The Kennedy Center Honors will move to a new location for the first time in its history: On December 7, the ceremony will be held at Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C. Deadline wrote, “Since Trump took over the center and ousted board members appointed by his predecessors, the center has seen a drop in ticket sales, while artists have canceled performances. The Washington Post and CNN have recently done deep dives on the dire state of Kennedy Center finances. Major shows ended in July, which had been the original time frame for when Trump and the center planned for the long-term closure for renovations.” In Edelman’s guest essay , headlined “I Loved Performing at the Kennedy Center. I May Never Do It Again,” the Paper actor and stand-up comic writes about the impact of Trump’s takeover on performers who once treasured booking gigs at the D.C. institution. “In the latest round of President Trump’s imposition of personal politics and self-promotion, he’s closed a huge chunk of the main building, saying it needs a costly renovation — which he will authorize only if the building bears his name,” Edelman writes. “Given that the Kennedy Center is a national memorial and not a hotel or a steak-by-mail company, legal challenges to a renaming are unlikely to be over soon.” Legal challenges notwithstanding, Edelman writes, “Theatergoers are already losing. In 2025, the vision Mr. Trump laid out to the board — newly stocked with political allies, loyalists and, worst of all, Lee Greenwood — was depressingly free of thought about curation. It was all about putting on shows that make money — even though the center’s programming was $40 million in the black during the last year of the Biden administration.” Edelman puts the center’s turmoil in personal terms from his perspective as both a performer and an audience member. “In recent years,” he writes, “when I would check the calendar or see shows there, I was struck by how diverse the programming was — but diverse in the underused, literal sense. Ballet. Comedy. Country. Opera. Hip-hop. Theater — from Guys and Dolls to the avant-garde. And honestly, in its diversity, I often found offerings that weren’t for me. Dull re-heatings of old plays, pedestrian touring stops for milquetoast musicals and Thai contemporary dance. Oof. But the not-for-me productions were part of the Kennedy Center’s appeal. The remit seemed to be not far-off from the Smithsonian’s down the street: art that was in the public interest and art that should be.” As a performer, “If you played the Kennedy Center, you’d meet the sweet weirdos who are like the sweet weirdos who program and promote theaters all around the country. Culture nerds and eggheads and snobs who care about bringing in the big headliners and also root around in the bargain bins at music festivals for up-and-comers an audience might like.” Now, he says, “The comedians and actors I know no longer talk about it like a venue you want to visit. The Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize — which Steve Martin, an honoree, once referred to as the only significant American award for comedy ‘apart from money’ — have been so thoroughly politicized as to be nearly worthless. I honestly feel bad for the talented people still performing there and the surely handcuffed staff doing their best to keep it all going.” The J ust For Us performer hasn’t entirely given up hope for the Kennedy Center entirely. “I have also noticed that there’s an election coming up,” he concludes. “And administrations don’t last forever. So maybe I’ll get to come back and perform next to the Potomac — for people who find me funny and for people who decide I’m not for them. Strangers, folks I know from high school, college students, locals, tourists. Sitting in the dark with groceries and their friends and other Americans; laughing, laughing, laughing.” ‘Beyond The Gates’ Scores Big In First Year; Red Carpet Photo Gallery Hello Sunshine Cuts Half Of Staff After Acquisition By Witherspoon & Mediawan ‘Clayface’ & ‘You Can See Everything’ Brawling For Halloween Weekend Crown Classic Horror Pics & TV Episodes, Scary Triple Bills, Final Girls, Monsters, More Read More About: Comments

title: What To Watch For As Networks Cover Midterm Election Night: More Data, More Coverage & More Competition
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Daytime Emmy Winners: ‘General Hospital’ Wins Sixth Best Drama Series In A Row; ‘Kelly Clarkson’ Takes Talk Series Trophy In Final Year Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted What To Watch For As Networks Cover Midterm Election Night: More Data, More Coverage & More Competition Attorney For CNN, MS NOW & Politico Talks About Why It’s Urgent To Stop Latest Trump White House Ban: “The Chilling Effect Is Immense” Paula Reid Joins MS NOW As Chief White House Reporter View All October 31, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise from top left: James Talarico, Ken Paxton, Troy Jackson, Susan Collins, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers Getty Images Networks are preparing for their most important night of the year, an Election Night next week that will feature more data, more bells and whistles and, perhaps most important, just more coverage than any recent midterm cycle. The robust plans across the linear landscape come as a blizzard of creators, podcasters and pundits on YouTube and elsewhere will be competing for eyeballs, offering their followers their own takes as the returns finally come in. Related Stories News Michael Douglas Predicts Electoral “Massacre” For Donald Trump In Midterms News Trump Celebrity Supporters: Famous Folks In Favor Of The 47th President Traditional media still has the vast resources, whether that means deploying teams in response to an expanding map or preparing for polling disruptions or election misinformation. The night looks to be as much a referendum on Donald Trump as it will be a consequential decision on who will control Congress and a majority of governor races. NBC News is planning 13 hours of coverage on the broadcast network, starting at 5 p.m. ET on Tuesday and running until 6 a.m. ET the next morning — the most ever the network has planned for the midterm. Watch on Deadline Hallie Jackson, who will kick off the evening just as the first exit poll findings are released, suggested that the interest this cycle warrants it, with the unpredictability from an expanding map. “Nobody can write the story of Election Night before the ballots are cast, and that includes us. I mean, nobody,” she said. “And so we just got to stay flexible, stay nimble and see what the night holds. That’s what makes, I think, our coverage so interesting because we’re right there with our audience, unpacking this as it happens.” As always, there will be a race to make major calls, with each network tasking separate decision desks to pore over the data. A difference is that for the first time since 2016, all the major networks will be relying on the same exit poll information, called The Voter Poll, from SSRS. Fox News anchor Bill Hemmer, who again will be at the network’s Big Board, said, “It’s great to be first; it’s a hell of a lot better to be right.” All of the networks are making efforts to keep viewers within their universe of streaming channels, digital platforms and social media accounts — a familiar refrain is “meeting viewers where they are.” This battle for eyeballs means, for instance, that Fox News will have an AI-powered chatbot on its app, while the Ruthless podcast will have a three-hour Election Night streaming special on Fox Nation and Fox News Digital. Hemmer said that for the viewer, “You turn on the TV in a moment’s notice and you’re like, ‘Where do I look?’ You’re sitting in your living room or you’re watching on your phone or whatever. Where do you put your attention? And that’s a big part of our job.” Most of the networks are promising unique content on subscription platforms and mobile apps, as they seek to keep viewers within their branded universe. As in recent cycles, networks will offer behind-the-scenes looks at activity, with NBC News again doing a livestream of Steve Kornacki tracking the results, known as the Kornacki Cam, while MS NOW will have the VelshiCast, a YouTube channel stream of its data expert, Ali Velshi. This follows a contest that the channel had in which participants could win a limited-edition “Velshi vest.” In addition to its linear coverage, CBS News is featuring the streaming Election 2026: The Nerd Show , hosted by Anthony Salvanto and Caitlin Huey-Burns, on CBS News 24/7, YouTube and other platforms. It’s designed to draw in political junkies looking for the latest in numbers, data and models. David Reiter, SVP of CBS News 24/7, said: “I know we will be doing an amazing show on CBS. But that kind of assumption that you’ll do it and people will come is not as operative as it used to be. So we had to think differently this year, and our first foray into that is The Nerd Show .” ABC News will be in a new studio at the network’s new headquarters, with a new set and a return to the legacy brand for election coverage, “Vote 2026.” ABC News Live will stream coverage throughout the day, and the new offerings include the app’s election playlist with a Verts feed, directing users to vertical video content. Seni Tienabeso, VP of ABC News Live and specialized units, said: “Viewers will be seeking out our straightforward approach and brand, and will come to look to us to decipher fact from fiction and know that we’re the ones that we’re going to be delivering the election results in a straightforward way.” He, too, said that the multiplatform offerings are essential because “we know that the audiences are fragmented and getting those from different places, so we’re trying to meet them where they are, and we think that we can do that.” CNN is planning round-the-clock coverage starting at midnight ET on Tuesday, with Elex Michaelson’s show from Los Angeles and coverage continuing throughout the early morning and the rest of the day. Among the other plans: John Berman and Harry Enten returning with the election evening show CNN Office Hours , a livestream that will include an audience Q&A. At the local level, Tegna is rolling out a new mobile app tailored to its 51 markets. Elsewhere, SiriusXM is planning around-the-clock coverage through its political channels, with Stephen A. Smith broadcasting live from Washington, D.C., on the POTUS Channel and Megyn Kelly hosting on her channel, among other coverage. Politico is going live with results and analysis for an Election Night stream from its newsroom. Piers Morgan is taking his YouTube series to Washington next week, with three nights of programs including a four-hour special. This will be the first Election Night for his company Uncensored, led by CEO Rashida Jones, formerly of MSNBC. C-SPAN is supplementing its Election Night coverage — featuring full coverage and Democracy Dashboard results on its flagship channel — with simulcasts of The Young Turks with Cenk Uygur on C-SPAN2 and the PBD Podcast , hosted by Patrick Bet-David, on C-SPAN 3, representing voices from the left and the right, respectively. C-SPAN CEO Sam Feist said: “The reality in 2026 America is that many Americans, particularly younger Americans, are consuming news and information from creators and from podcasts, and we decided that this would be an opportunity on Election Night, when we had two available networks. Because if you’re interested in politics and public affairs, you’re watching on Election Night.” Creators in the game This will be another cycle in which podcasters, independent journalists and creators will have a heavy presence on Election Night, reacting to the results or in certain cases providing their our streams of data. The Bulwark will feature a non-paywalled livestream that includes The Next Level podcast at 7 p.m. ET, and plans for more panels throughout the evening, with updates from reporters in Ohio, Michigan, Texas, Georgia and from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. The media company, which has been expanding in Trump 2.0, has a lineup including Tim Miller, Sarah Longwell, Bill Kristol and Jonathan V. Last. For the first time, Jubilee Media will be hosting live coverage on YouTube, co-hosted by David Mauricio and Austin Julio Broughton of The Split . Two former network mainstays-turned-creators, Chuck Todd and Chris Cillizza, will host The Projection along with Decision Desk HQ, relying on the latter’s data to make their own calls. That just scratches the surface when it comes to plans for independent podcasters and hosts. C-SPAN’s simulcasts of Uygur and Bet-David will feature their shows before live audiences. Feist said that he was impressed by their production values and that it was a chance “to expose their audiences to C-SPAN,” while noting that the live coverage will be a case of “traditional media meets new media.” “It’s a recognition that these voices are really important in the body politic,” Feist said. CBS News’ Reiter said that one of the rationales for The Nerd Show was a recognition that there is demand for a “deep dive into the data of particular appeal to those with a fervent interest in politics. ” Mark Lima, VP and Washington bureau chief for the network, said that The Nerd Show “is a comfortable extension of kind of how we try to reach audiences all the time. And I think we’ll do it in a way that’s that’s kind of very special.” David Chalian, SVP and Washington bureau chief for CNN, said that its coverage “is going to be totally different because of the way in which our viewers are consuming information. That’s been evolving over time, but the sort of fully multimodal expression of our Election Night coverage is going to reflect that reality.” He added: “I think all those influencers are also part of the political fabric now, and they are part of the conversation. And some of them have huge followings, and some of them play to one party or the other in their audiences. All of that is sort of part of the the political conversation. But I don’t know that they will all have the amount of actual data coming in the way that CNN does.” MS NOW will be doing its first major Election Night since the split from Comcast last year, as it has built up its own newsroom. Shawna Thomas, who joined as political director in June, said: “I’m pretty confident that we know how to make this interesting. We know how to make this smart. We know how not to fall into traps that sometimes other news organizations do on TV on Election Day.” She added: “This is about voters voting, and so I mean the polls help us make decisions up until that day. But then let’s look at the real numbers that are coming out that night.” NBC News’ Jackson said: “Our north star is very much what’s happening on the ground with the data and with the results. We want to bring people into that. You’re not gonna see a lot of just yapping around the deck. It’s a lot of focusing on the results coming in, what they mean, what indications they can give us about some of the races that are still outstanding.” In other words, after months of commentary and predictions about what is going to happen, the results take center stage. Chris Stirewalt, politics editor at NewsNation , said his network’s approach will be “NFL Red Zone-style,” with a lot of calls of races. “It’s going to be transparent, and it’s going to be race after race after race,” he said. “The time for spin, the time for bloviation is over.” In contrast to other networks, NewsNation is partnered with Decision Desk HQ, which was the first to call the presidential race for Donald Trump in 2024. Stirewalt added: “If you are at a point where you need to be soothed or gentled by your Election Night coverage, and you don’t want to hear the bad news, then I’m sure there are places that you can go where people will tell you what you want to hear or don’t tell you anything at all. But I think most people would rather just be told, right? I think most people would rather just know what’s going on.” The networks also point to another resource they will have: Reporting throughout the day across the country, interviewing voters. Although anecdotal, that information can at times be a tell. MS NOW’s Thomas said: “We have to be clear on what our story is. We have to have to be clear on really trying to hone in on hearing from the voters. And we have to be clear on [the fact that] we have the bells and whistles to make interesting television and offer people the option. But it’s all competition.” Big data dives The Voter Poll will take the temperature across every state with a Senate or governor’s race — 45 in all — giving most of the networks a wider scope of information on why people voted the way they did. That is a contrast to previous midterms , when such information came from battleground states. ABC News’ Tienabeso said, “There’s more data than there’s ever been. “There’s going to be a lot more incoming to take in but also process and make understandable to the viewer. It’s really exciting, but that is a challenge,” he said. The network will have a simulator that can calculate odds — and now they change — as results come in. Jenn Metz, executive producer of special events and news specials planning, said: “We’ve really been tracking over the past couple of years something that we’re calling the voter shift, and that’s how we can quantify voters in the states either voting more toward the right or more toward the left.” That was a trend in 2024, with a huge shift toward the Republicans, and this midterm may see one toward the Democrats, she noted. The night will reflect what has become commonplace through election season — a focus on probabilities and win percentages, giving a peek at what decision desks are seeing and which way they are leaning before making a call. CNN will debut Sightline, a real-time assessment of who is ahead in major races, that Chalian said will explain “how our analysts and data experts are able to project races or not, and why.” He said it will “give users and audiences an inside look as to why we’re not at the confidence level to be at to make a projection yet, but we see this race as favoring one candidate or the other and explain why that is at that moment in time.” CBS News will have the FutureCast, giving insight into where House and Senate control are headed, changing as more results come in but also with a margin-of-error caveat. Reiter said that the FutureCast was another step in being “much more transparent” about the information their data desk has. He said: “I hope you’ll never hear someone say, ‘It’s too early to call” or “There’s not enough information.’ We’ll we’ll provide you with at least a race rating, and then our FutureCast will tell you where our models think the night will end up.” Fox News is expanding its use of augmented reality and voice recognition that will call up graphics via a key word, like a state, county or certain demographics. “What matters in the end is what the numbers are for the red team and the blue team. Period. Full stop,” Hemmer said. “But since we are trying to tell a story in an interesting way, and technology has enabled us to imagine new things when it comes to our storytelling, that’s why we’re incorporating these new features.” Hemmer said that on Election Night, “I find the biggest challenge is to frame the story as accurately as you can, given the intense flow of data you are seeing in real time. And then [you have to decide], how do you present this story in a way that makes sense, is understandable and is also accurate.” Prediction markets CBS News will feature data from Kalshi, its prediction market sponsor, reflecting the increasing presence of betting in political races. Reiter said that the prediction market will be another data point, and “it’ll be really interesting on Election Night to see not only you know as the votes come in, as we get the exit polls, but to see where are the prediction markets and how are they changing, and to be able to discuss with some of their really smart folks why they think that’s happening.” CNN’s Chalian said that prediction markets “have grown more sophisticated over time and have certainly entered the chat, if you will, in this election season in a way they had not before.” But he cautioned that it was not a “standalone data point. It’s one of a gazillion data points out there, and so you got to feed it into the entire mix of everything.” The midterm also could be a test as to how much importance prediction markets have in gauging voter sentiment. NewsNation’s Stirewalt said that “we have a lot of evidence now that tells us that betting markets are lagging indicators, not leading indicators” and not “materially different from Fan Duel or DraftKings.” Fox News’ Hemmer said: “There could be value in them. I’m not entirely disregarding them, but I would much rather rely on data that I am seeing and that our team is receiving rather than an outside source to give me a forecast that I can’t prove.” Election Fraud: Real or Fake? Networks say they are prepared for the possibility of election disputes, whether that be in poll disruptions, legal challenges or fraud claims, with reports that the Justice Department plans to send an expanded number of election monitors to polling locations. Most networks have teams of legal reporters and election-integrity experts at the ready. Just as important is context. ABC News’ Tienabeso said that includes knowing whether something that is happening is “of national significance or this is something that happens every election cycle.” Metz said that also includes the vote count and informing viewers that “what we’re seeing is is what it what it should be, and to just keep reassuring the viewers as the night goes on that if in fact what’s going on is normal, this is normal, and this is how you know the the vote process works. We’re watching democracy play out in real time.” CBS News’ Lima said that their voter-monitoring Democracy Desk is “going to be watching very carefully for any anomalies that might happen, anything that might affect the votes in various states. That’s something in these last couple election cycles we really had to pay attention to as well. And obviously, we’ve seen the start of some of that and accusations already, and we’re going to be paying really close attention to the vote.” The Expanding Map This week came new polling showing an unexpectedly tight race in South Carolina, where Republican Darline Graham, appointed to the seat after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham , is running against Democrat Annie Andrews. The expanding map of close races, particularly in the Senate, has forced networks to dispatch more reporters to spots deemed safe for Republicans six months ago. MS NOW’s Thomas said that “even as we started to lay out where we wanted reporters for Election Night and the weekend before the last round of campaigning, that list has changed a little bit over the course of the month as we make sure we are in the right places to tell the story of this election.” C-SPAN’s Feist said that its Road to the Capital project started with about 60-70 races, but that number has “expanded significantly.” “We’ve had to deploy additional resources and to cover races we never thought we would be covering on 2026 Election Night,” he said. The network is relying on their crews and embeds as well as other news organizations to capture feeds from dozens of campaign headquarters. Just the planning the days before the election has been a scramble, as Trump rallies for Kansas and Iowa were canceled in favor of tele-rallies, then they were back on. “The map is challenging because so much of it this year is playing on what had been reliably Republican turf,” CNN’s Chalian said. “So it’s not as if you can approach the Election Night [by assuming] ‘Oh, the red states will stay red, the blue states will stay blue. Here are the purple states.’ Instead, the actual battlefield of competition is taking place in a lot of deep-red-territory states, states that Donald Trump won by double digits just two years ago, and they’re now the ones that are like going to be determinative, and so it sort of gives it a different kind of element, some new places we have not necessarily been focused on at sort of the heart of political competition in America in the last few years.” NewsNation’s Stirewalt said: “We have, relatively speaking, such a wide range of potential scenarios that we just have to be prepared for all of it, right? So given the data that we have, we could be looking at a red wall. We could be looking at a blue wave. We could be looking at a blue tsunami. All are in play, and some more probable than others, but all in play. title: Dubai-Based Director Faisal Hashmi Launches Spine Drop Pictures & Inaugural Horror Slate
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Daytime Emmy Winners: ‘General Hospital’ Wins Sixth Best Drama Series In A Row; ‘Kelly Clarkson’ Takes Talk Series Trophy In Final Year Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai-Based Director Faisal Hashmi Launches Spine Drop Pictures & Inaugural Horror Slate ‘The Sun Never Sets’ Sells Out For Capture As Focus Features Swoops On Multiple Territories Forest Whitaker Joins Rachid Bouchareb’s ‘Boomerang Atomic’ As EP Ahead Of DOC NYC Screening View All October 31, 2026 3:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Faisal Hashmi, Spine Drop Pictures logo Spine Drop Pictures EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a nicely timed company announcement for Halloween . Dubai-based indie director and writer Faisal Hashmi has officially launched genre-focused production company Spine Drop Pictures and unveiled its inaugural slate of three horror features. Hashmi has won fans over his 15-year career with a collection of 10 contained, high-concept genre shorts with chilling twists, including as Amber , Wicken and Skipped , which have screened at scores of film festivals and generated more than three million combined views on YouTube. Related Stories News Dark Sky Films Takes U.S. Rights To Prize-Winning Emirati Horror 'The Vile' Festivals Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Alongside directing, he also recently took co-writing credits on Emirati director Ali F. Mostafa’s long-awaited feature City of Life Continuum , a sequel to his breakout 2009 debut City of Life . Watch on Deadline Hashmi is also attached to write and direct English-language, time-loop horror-thriller Fractal , starring Jason Flemyng and Gabriela Vargas, which is being produced by Vienna-based Pont Pictures and is targeting a 2027 shoot in Serbia. Hashmi’s strategy for Spine Drop Pictures is to focus on high concept, commercially oriented genre pictures, budgeted at below $1 million and tapping into his experience of working on a tight budget with his short films. “I’ve always looked at how can I tell an amazing story with less locations, fewer resources, but still make the concept so strong that it doesn’t feel like I’m trying to make an expensive movie for cheap, but rather a movie that feels contained and is made in the best way to make it in the first place,” he told Deadline. The inaugural slate spans Off Plan , Cinde r and Latching , which have been written and will be directed by Hashmi. Off Plan is an interconnected horror anthology featuring six stories unfolding across Dubai over the course of a single night. Hashmi has designed a modular shooting approach so that the six segments can be filmed as separate short-form productions that can be scheduled independently, allowing for greater flexibility and cost efficiency through shared crew and production resources. Cinder is billed as a gritty supernatural thriller set against the unforgiving remote mountain landscapes of the UAE . It expands on Hashmi’s award-winning 2020 short film Amber, in which a barber in a remote UAE highway town finds himself up against a vicious kidnapper who has abducted a young girl. The short won best film at the UAE’s Al Ain Film Festival. Hashmi describes Latching as a feminist possession-revenge horror film unfolding over the course of a single harrowing night in Karachi, Pakistan, where it is being developed for production. Longtime UAE resident Hashmi is of Pakistani descent. “We’ve seen what’s possible internationally with the success of low-budget, high-concept horror films like Obsession , Undertone and Good Boy . In an emerging independent film market like the UAE, I think that approach is especially important. We need films that aren’t just creatively ambitious, but commercially viable, with a realistic potential for profitability and international appeal,” continued Hashmi on his strategy. “A sustainable film industry isn’t built on getting one expensive film financed. It’s built on making films that can find audiences, recover their investments and help finance the next one. That’s the thinking behind Spine Drop Pictures.” Hashimi says Spine Drop Pictures is exploring opportunities for slate investment, international co-productions, strategic financing and distribution partnerships as it advances its inaugural features. ‘Beyond The Gates’ Scores Big In First Year; Red Carpet Photo Gallery Hello Sunshine Cuts Half Of Staff After Acquisition By Witherspoon & Mediawan ‘Clayface’ & ‘You Can See Everything’ Brawling For Halloween Weekend Crown Classic Horror Pics & TV Episodes, Scary Triple Bills, Final Girls, Monsters, More Read More About: Comments

title: Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: “It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 31, 2026 3:13am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Macklemore at the Free Palestine Tour in London on Oct. 30, 2026 Photo credit: Zoe Rain Macklemore brought the final night of his Free Palestine Tour to London on Friday, telling a U.K. audience: “I don’t believe that staying silent is brave.” The sold-out event at the capital’s OVO Arena Wembley boasted a crowd of over 12,500 people, who cheered and screamed as the U.S. rapper spoke. The gigs come weeks after he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour for expressing his pro-Palestine views on stage. Sheeran later said it was a promoter decision to drop Macklemore, and that venues set to host the concerts threatened to pull out if Macklemore was on the bill. Related Stories Movies 'Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting' Review: Whimsical Chinese Film Explores Myth and History Through a Series of Tasty Treats Business Japan's Anime Industry Hits a Record High of $28 Billion in 2025 In response, Macklemore launched his own benefit concert with acts in the British capital such as Aja Monet, Cure for Paranoia, Dana Saleh, Nemahsis, Lucas Jones, Paloma Faith, Roze, Shadia Mansour and Vic Mensa. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg was among the guest speakers, along with Hollywood superstars Mark Ruffalo, Susan Sarandon, Javier Bardem, Cynthia Nixon, as well as Melissa Barrera and Julian Casablancas, dialing in remotely. “It was more uncomfortable for me to stay silent than to say something,” said Macklemore about the situation with Sheeran. “And I just want to say, I don’t believe that saying something is brave. I don’t believe that saying something is courageous. I believe that saying something is human. And those children in Gaza are our children. There is no separation.” He continued: “I want to say thank you to every single soul that is in here tonight who decided to step up, leave their couch, be in community, be reminded and feel what that frequency of love feels like.” Macklemore added about the 50 members of the British House of Lords who urged the U.K. government to ban his concert: “Regardless of what the 50 Lords have to say, this is a story of equality for all human beings around this earth.” All proceeds from the concerts in Dublin, Paris and London will go toward organizations supporting Palestinian communities through humanitarian relief, medical care, education, advocacy, policy change and community initiatives, according to the rapper’s team. Popular Irish acts Hozier and Kneecap were included on the lineup in Dublin , as was Boega, Sheeran’s backing band that pulled out of the Loop Tour in solidarity with Macklemore. After widespread backlash, Sheeran was emotional as he addressed the controversy onstage in Philadelphia last month : “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said. “My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. […] What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7th was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate.” Sheeran told the crowd: “Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” The singer added that he was “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance. […] This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world.” According to numbers from the British Red Cross , the death toll in Gaza is over 69,000. Almost 1,200 Israelis were killed in the Oct. 7 attack in 2023. THR

title: Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59
full_text: × Oct 31, 2026 2:33am PT Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59 By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Sourav Ganguly’s ‘Bigg Boss Bangla’ Among Highlights as Indian Media Giant JioStar Revenues Climb 10% 9 hours ago How Keanu Reeves Landed in Stop-Motion Samurai Epic ‘Hidari’ – and Why S.S. Rajamouli Wanted to Know How It Was Made 10 hours ago Georgia’s ‘Guria’ Wins Best Film at Asia Pacific Screen Awards as Thailand’s Sompot Chidgasornpongse Takes Director Prize 11 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta , whose credits include the crime thriller “ Kaante ,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-starring “Kaabil,” has died following a fall at his Mumbai residence on Oct. 30. He was 59, according to the Press Trust of India . Director Milap Zaveri, a longtime friend of Gupta who worked on the dialogue for “Kaante,” confirmed the death to PTI. “It is true that he passed away. He fell and hit his head,” Zaveri said. Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference Police in Mumbai’s Versova neighborhood have filed an accidental death report. Deputy Commissioner of Police Purushottam Karad told the Free Press Journal that members of Gupta’s family were sleeping when the incident occurred and became aware of it the following morning. “The family has not raised any suspicion or lodged a complaint,” Karad said. Gupta was a prominent exponent of the glossy, action-driven Hindi-language crime thriller, bringing a visual sensibility heavily indebted to Hollywood to an industry traditionally dominated by melodrama and musicals. His career behind the camera began with “Aatish: Feel the Fire” in 1994, featuring Sanjay Dutt and Aditya Pancholi. He subsequently directed “Ram Shastra,” “Jung” and “Khauff,” developing an enduring professional relationship with Dutt that extended across 10 films, including projects Gupta produced. The filmmaker achieved one of his biggest successes with “Kaante” in 2002, assembling Amitabh Bachchan , Dutt, Suniel Shetty, Mahesh Manjrekar, Lucky Ali and Kumar Gaurav for a Los Angeles-set heist thriller about a group of criminals planning a bank robbery. The production was filming in the city when the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, forced changes to its location schedule, as Gupta recounted in a Rediff interview the following year. The film’s similarities to Quentin Tarantino ‘s “Reservoir Dogs” drew considerable attention, although Tarantino subsequently expressed admiration for “Kaante” in a 2007 interview covered by the Times of India . Gupta received a Filmfare nomination for best director. Questions about the influence of international films followed Gupta throughout his career, and he made little secret of his willingness to draw inspiration from existing material. Responding to accusations of plagiarism in his 2002 Rediff interview, he said he would “beg, borrow and steal from any medium” in pursuit of a compelling story. Several of his subsequent films reflected that philosophy. “Musafir” (2004) bore similarities to Oliver Stone’s “U Turn,” while the Dutt and John Abraham thriller “Zinda” (2006) attracted particular controversy over its resemblance to Park Chan-wook’s South Korean film “Oldboy.” The Korean production company Show East told Star News in November 2005 that it was considering legal remedies should the completed Hindi film prove substantially similar to the original. Gupta later directed “Jazbaa” (2015), an adaptation of the Korean thriller “Seven Days” that brought Aishwarya Rai Bachchan back to the screen. Gupta also established himself as a producer through White Feather Films. The company’s credits included “Shootout at Lokhandwala” (2007), “Acid Factory,” “Pankh” and the anthology “Dus Kahaniyaan,” which Gupta also directed. He returned to the gangster genre with “Shootout at Wadala” (2013), a prequel to “Shootout at Lokhandwala” drawing on S. Hussain Zaidi’s nonfiction book “Dongri to Dubai.” With “Kaabil” in 2017, Gupta directed Hrithik Roshan as a visually impaired man pursuing vengeance, in a film produced by Rakesh Roshan. His later work included the crime drama “Mumbai Saga” (2021), a T-Series co-production whose theatrical prospects were affected by a renewed surge in COVID-19 infections. His producing credits also extended to “Visfot” (2024), a Hindi adaptation of the Venezuelan thriller “Rock, Paper, Scissors.” Colleagues remembered Gupta’s contributions to the industry’s visual and promotional vocabulary. “Raees” director Rahul Dholakia described him on X as a stylish filmmaker and “maybe the first to present trailers and cut promos to pitch the film idea to actors and distributors.” Director Kunal Kohli, whose films include “Fanaa,” recalled a conversation with Gupta only a few weeks before his death, as well as their time together as members of an awards jury. “You had many more films and many years to go,” Kohli wrote . Dutt posted : “Gupts, my brother. I still cannot believe that you are gone. We have shared so much together, so many memories and so many years of friendship. You have always been family to me, and that will never change. I will miss you, our conversations and all the times we spent together.” Sound designer Resul Pookutty, Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” wrote : “What a terrible and shocking news for me personally and our friends and family. 25 Years of working together. I’m not able to process this… we will miss you, one of the sanest voices from mainstream Hindi cinema… May your soul rest in eternal peace.” Beyond filmmaking, Gupta maintained an active presence on X, frequently offering pointed commentary on the Hindi film industry’s creative and commercial direction. He had also begun discussing a possible return to one of his best-known properties. Following the resolution of a dispute involving White Feather Films and Pritish Nandy Communications over “Kaante,” Gupta revealed on the “InControversial” podcast earlier this year that he had developed the foundations of a sequel. He said the story for “Kaante 2” had been worked out “at a very base level” and that he intended to begin writing the screenplay. Gupta is survived by his wife and two children. title: Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass
full_text: × Oct 31, 2026 1:40am PT Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass By Mark Schilling Plus Icon Mark Schilling Japan Correspondent Latest Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass 6 hours ago Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’ 8 hours ago AI Can Critique Shakespeare but Can’t Write It, Russo Brothers’ AGBO Execs Tell Tokyo Market 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images The Tokyo International Film Festival ’s Tokyo Talk program presented a masterclass with Zeze Takahisa , director of the festival’s opening film, “Sukiyaki.” Held before a full-house crowd at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, the talk focused on Zeze’s early “pink” (softcore porn) and indie films, followed by questions about his more recent work. Born in 1960 in Oita Prefecture, Zeze joined a pink film production company in 1986 and worked as an assistant director. He made his directorial debut in 1989 with “Extracurricular Activity: Rape,” for which he won the Pink Grand Prix Award for Best New Director. Together with Sano Kazuhiro, Sato Toshiki and Sato Hisayasu, Zeze was hailed as one of the “Four Heavenly Kings of Pink.” Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference Pink films screened in specialized theaters for an exclusively male audience, and directors had to insert a bed scene every 10 minutes or so. “I’ve always been pretty firm in my convictions,” said Zeze. “Starting from the early 1990s the culture shifted and I had more freedom to say what I wanted. That kind of thing was important to me.” At the time, Zeze was interested in stories about female criminals. “It’s just different from the male perspective,” he said. “The motives behind the crimes and so on. I found it fascinating.” Scripted by Zeze, “Extracurricular Activity: Rape” was about delinquent high school girls who hang out at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and battle the yakuza. Zeze gave it the “private” title “Go to Haneda and You Will See Kids Dressed Like Pirates Ready to Attack.” Asked about a 1994 pink, “Genuine Lesbians: Embarrassing Positions” (Zeze’s own title: “Fallen Angels in September”), Zeze said the film, which was about female soulmates, reflected the interest he described as “this whole mysticism thing” shared by many young people then. “Searching for past lives became a sort of trend, and people started seeking connections to this different world,” he added. “I thought that maybe I could make a movie centered around something like that.” Zeze said the “Four Heavenly Kings” moniker came from a pink theater “in Toyama – or maybe Ishikawa – I can’t remember.” It reminded Zeze and the other “kings” of “Nouvelle Vague” – a tag that gave critical and commercial cachet to its members. “So we figured that, rather than work as individuals, we should debut under a group name,” he said. “We decided to use the ‘Four Heavenly Kings’ label to our advantage.” The “kings” films were also shown in retrospectives at the Rotterdam festival and elsewhere abroad. “Actually, the overseas reception came first, and then it was sort of re-imported” back to Japan, Zeze said. Meanwhile, in Japan, the “kings” and other pink film directors still had to incorporate a certain amount of eros. “No one was telling us to stop doing these politically sensitive things,” said Zeze. “It was just wonderful… there really was a lot of freedom back then.” Also, pink film directors were not confined to a porn ghetto. “Things weren’t standardized back then,” Zeze said. “I worked with directors from my generation who had diverse backgrounds, like Aoyama Shinji and Suzuki Takuji. We’d get together either because we’d met by chance or because we wanted to create something interesting.” In 1997 Zeze made his mainstream debut with the teen horror “Kokkuri-san” but continued to alternate between pink and mainstream films for the next decade. In 2010 he released his most ambitious film to date, “Heaven’s Story,” a 278-minute revenge drama that screened in the Forum section of the Berlin Film Festival, where it won the FIPRESCI Prize. “It was different from a so-called ‘ordinary movie,’” Zeze said. “I’d been working on commercial films until then, but I realized I had to do something else. Personally, I felt a sense of urgency – or maybe a sense of crisis – that things weren’t going well, and that’s what pushed me to take on this challenge.” There’s a lot of talk, Zeze said, about how difficult it is to make a film unless it’s adapted from source material. “But the movies we actually found interesting or the ones I personally found entertaining were all originals.” Zeze himself has made commercial films with stories sourced from existing IP, such as the hit 2016 two-part mystery/suspense “64,” which was based on a bestselling novel, but said, “The industry is too focused on the ‘source material market.’ They think that if the source material is selling well, they should adapt it.” “So I feel that pursuing original concepts and making original films is incredibly important right now,” he added. “They have a unique, compelling strength.” Blackpink and ‘White Lotus’ Star Lisa Documentary ‘Always Lalisa’ Sets Global Release Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations Alexander Ludwig on ‘Unabomber’ Movie, His ‘Hunger Games’ Death Scene and ‘White Lotus’ Season 4: ‘It’s F—ing Wild’ France Riots Put Hollywood Shoots on Alert as Curfews Disrupt Movie Theaters: It ‘Has Now Been Flagged as a Problem Area’ Loading comments...

title: Japan’s Film Funds Look Beyond Production Committees to Build New Financing Models
full_text: × Oct 31, 2026 1:15am PT Japan’s Film Funds Look Beyond Production Committees to Build New Financing Models By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest Annecy Winner ‘The Violinist’ Found Its Italian Co-Producers at Tokyo Market, Director Ervin Han Tells Anime Co-Production Panel 1 day ago Japan’s Anime Market Hits Record $28.2 Billion as Local Sales Surge 1 day ago ‘Godzilla Minus One’ U.S. Success ‘Wasn’t a Strategy; We Just Tried,’ Says Toho CEO at Tokyo Festival 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lin Ying-Hsuan Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the industry. But it can also cap budgets at what the industry itself can raise, make it harder for overseas investors to take part and slow decisions when every rights holder must agree. At a panel at TIFFCOM , the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival , speakers examined whether film funds can ease those limits while still fitting Japan’s market. Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference “Film Funds in Japan: What Works, What Doesn’t, and What Comes Next” featured Kii Muneyuki, CEO and producer of K2 Pictures, which works with filmmakers including Kore-eda Hirokazu , Miike Takashi and Nishikawa Miwa; Ibe Tomonobu, CEO of Questry, a Tokyo startup that uses digital securities to fund anime and other Japanese content; Nakagawa Keita, managing director at MUFG Bank; and Motoyanagi Yusuke, partner at law firm Nishimura & Asahi. Kii presented K2P Film Fund I as one example of a new structure. The fund closed in February at about JPY5 billion ($32 million) and aims to back around 50 films over seven years. It is a blind pool, meaning investors commit money before the films are chosen. Its investors include MUFG, the Development Bank of Japan and other financial institutions and companies, and a greenlight committee oversees project approvals. Kii said five films had been released in theaters in 2026. Kii said a central question for film funds is how to return revenue to creators, including income from streaming and other windows after a film’s theatrical run. He also said it is hard to rely on overseas box office, and that Japanese companies need to build businesses beyond distribution. The panel compared financing structures in the U.S. and South Korea. In the U.S., producers combine presales with completion guarantees to help secure bank loans. A completion guarantee covers delivery of a film on budget and on schedule, rather than its commercial performance. South Korea relies on public-private support, with government-backed guarantees helping projects get bank financing. Nakagawa presented a Japan-specific feasibility study commissioned by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. MUFG was selected to carry it out on March 31. Running through February 2027, the study will use real-world data to develop valuation and completion-guarantee models, and test the full process from application and review to contract drafting. The study assesses feasibility and does not guarantee that financing or completion guarantees will become available. The discussion closed with four priorities: regulation, capital, creators and cross-border business. These include clarifying which regulations should be expanded and when, combining debt with subsidies and completion guarantees, and building creator returns into fund structures. Speakers also pointed to language and tax hurdles to cross-border investment, including “permanent establishment” rules that can make international investors liable for Japanese tax. title: Japan’s New 2027 Anime Award Should Put Creators in the Spotlight, Industry Leaders Say at Tokyo Market
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 11:51pm PT Japan’s New 2027 Anime Award Should Put Creators in the Spotlight, Industry Leaders Say at Tokyo Market By Kambole Campbell Plus Icon Kambole Campbell Latest Japan’s New 2027 Anime Award Should Put Creators in the Spotlight, Industry Leaders Say at Tokyo Market 8 hours ago Taiwanese Feature ‘Uncle’ Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market Awards 1 day ago Aliens, Dinosaurs and a Father’s Death: ‘Kefi’ Director Saito Kisin Brings a Surreal Take on Grief to Tokyo 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kawakami Takashi A new Japanese anime award planned for 2027 should put the people who make anime in the spotlight, industry leaders said at TIFFCOM , the market of the Tokyo International Film Festival . The session was moderated by Fujitsu Ryota, programming advisor for the festival’s animation section. Shimizu Akira, a director of the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), is president and representative director of A-1 Pictures. He was joined by Studio Chizu president Saito Yuichiro, producer of “The Girl Who Leapt Through Time,” “Summer Wars” and “Wolf Children,” and Saito Masaya, chief manager of Toho’s animation division and planning group leader. Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference The award’s name and outline will be revealed Nov. 2 at the closing event of Tokyo Anime Next, the festival that organized the session. Co-hosted by the AJA and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, Tokyo Anime Next runs Oct. 30–Nov. 2 in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro district, with several events at TIFFCOM. The 2027 launch date has yet to be confirmed, and the panelists stressed that their views were not the award’s official positions. “Creators should be highlighted – and they should be put in the limelight,” Shimizu said when asked about the timing of the launch. Saito Masaya said Toho had helped work on the concept for the award, and agreed that creators should be highlighted. He added that the award could give fans a more direct connection to the people behind anime’s global popularity. The company wants to “help achieve a wider reach to anime fans and help give them a wider perspective,” he said, bringing them closer to different creative styles and approaches. Saito Yuichiro, a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, said an award is only one part of what the Academy does. “There are many different branches of work beyond the award,” he said. “The Academy Award in the United States is a domestic award, but it now has a global membership. They also provide training, and try to create a sort of succession plan for the industry. This kind of philosophy is the backbone for the award.” Ideally, the panelists said, financial support and training would also be among the building blocks of the new award. Saito Masaya said he hoped the award “can contribute to the changing of the ways audience enjoy anime.” He wants fans “to notice a certain aspect and ask who is behind this,” he added. Shimizu said the need to showcase the value of Japanese animation was “one of the key phrases.” “Japanese anime has a very unique workflow and processes, so who does what and who evaluates what, and who delivers those, and how are they embraced and valued by the audience,” he said. The panel noted that some awards have already picked up on that uniqueness. The Annie Awards have added a best international anime production for TV/media category for their 54th edition. “Japanese anime is a standalone established category,” Shimizu said, “anime is different from Disney, it is different from Pixar.” He said the new award should reflect those differences by spotlighting the creators who work on each part of an anime’s production. “For a layperson, the beauty of the anime can’t be expressed clearly in words,” he said. Saito Yuichiro said the world has two major trends. “The first one is this European Art History, generated from that long history and value system, and the worldwide large-scale trends centered in the United States. The world is composed of these two systems,” he said. He asked whether Asia could build its own equivalent “aesthetics and value system,” and whether an awards body could help bring an Asian voice into a system he sees as dominated by Europe and the U.S. “Borderlessness is very important, what I’d hope is to blur the boundaries between these areas of the world with these awards,” he said. title: Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’
full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 11:40pm PT Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’ By Mark Schilling Plus Icon Mark Schilling Japan Correspondent Latest Pink Film Veteran Zeze Takahisa Champions Original Stories at Tokyo Masterclass 6 hours ago Ozu Shapes Mishima Yukiko’s Tokyo Competition Title ‘Two Cigarettes, Three Nights’ 8 hours ago AI Can Critique Shakespeare but Can’t Write It, Russo Brothers’ AGBO Execs Tell Tokyo Market 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mark Schilling Known for her dark relationship dramas, including the 2017 multiple-award-winner “Dear Etranger,” Mishima Yukiko has taken a different approach with her latest film, “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights,” which is in competition at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival . Based on a 2014 novel by Chihaya Akane, it stars Matsuoka Mayu as Kanna, a picture book illustrator who has tired of her nice-but-boring live-in boyfriend (Inoue Yuki) while having nothing but a physical connection with her cynical married lover (Nakajima Ayumu). Related Stories ‘God of War’s’ Bruno Velazquez, ‘Mandalorian & Grogu’s’ Hal Hickel Detail Cinema-Gaming Crossover at View Conference Then a close friend from her college days, Haseo (Narita Ryo), reenters her life after a gap of seven years and once again becomes her confidant. Now a salesman for a drug company and still single, Haseo is something of a womanizer, though he keeps his relationship with Kanna strictly platonic. Shot in Kyoto, Hiroshima and Toyama Prefecture, the film makes screenwriter Sawai Kaori’s talky script feel visually dynamic, while avoiding cliché shots in Kyoto and Hiroshima, two of Japan’s most famous tourist destinations. Instead of posing against temples and cherry blossoms, the two principals stroll along a riverbank or on railroad tracks as they renew their friendship – and flirt with something more. “When deciding on a location, it’s not just about picking a ‘pretty’ spot,” says Mishima in an interview at Tokyo Midtown, the main festival site. “Rather it’s more about choosing a place where the scene comes to life.” “Also, the novel has a lot of scenes set inside a coffee shop, but in the movie (Kanna and Haseo) are walking just about the whole time,” she adds. Years ago, she and a male friend spent more time walking together than sitting inside a shop and talking, she recalls. “We didn’t talk about our worries and troubles – we’d walk until dawn, just chatting about trivial things.” “Trivial” is not the word to describe the film’s dialogue, but it has a bantering tone, as well as an unfiltered honesty. At the same time, Kanna and Haseo don’t face each other right away. “I didn’t want them to do that until a certain point,” says Mishima. “I wanted them to always be looking in the same direction. So when they go into a ramen shop, they are sitting side by side at a counter. The same with buses and trains – they sit next to each other, looking in the same direction.” A big influence in her shotmaking style, Mishima says, is Ozu Yasujiro, who often filmed characters side by side or even making the same motions in unison. “I love how he captures the way people move within the flow of Japanese life, without cutting the shot, creating a sense of wonder,” she says. “He is also brilliant in how he makes a grand narrative emerge from small, personal moments, so I’ve been greatly influenced by that as well. My film starts from that personal perspective, but then it kind of opens up to the world.” The film’s first act hints at sex comedy, and Mishima cast both of her leads – Matsuoka (“Tremble All You Want”) and Narita (“Convenience Story”) – with their comic abilities in mind. But she has crafted something more intimate and complex, with an ending open to interpretation. “I thought that having a good sense for comedy was essential for the long dialogue scenes,” says Mishima. “They require a sense of rhythm and actors with a feel for comedy have it. It makes a huge difference.” The film is no lighthearted laugh fest: Kanna and Haseo are not always likable characters, acting in ways selfish, callous and even cruel. “I think movies should be able to portray all kinds of people and tell all kinds of stories,” says Mishima. “And it’s good to have characters that represent all kinds of people, too.” “I think viewers will probably be able to relate to their emotions,” she adds. “They’ll be able to find a part of themselves – ‘Oh, I’ve felt this way too.’ That’s what makes a good actor. No matter how bad the person they’re portraying is, you end up understanding them or rather you can’t help but feel the way they do. That’s their charm.” Other characters add their perspectives, such as a surly bartender who is close to Haseo and thinks Kanna is hurting him, and Kanna’s jaded college friend who freely admits to cheating on her husband and sympathizes with Kanna’s infidelities. “I wanted to present the story in a multi-layered way,” says Mishima. “The film’s Japanese title is ‘The Male Friend,’ but it gradually drifts away from that theme. It’s more a story about what Kanna comes to see. By spending time with Haseo, she gains a perspective that lets her see not just herself but the world.” Kanna’s art also changes. In sharp contrast to the commercial hack work that pays her bills, she completes a painting that grows out of her three eventful days with Haseo. “What I want to convey is embedded in that final painting,” says Mishima. “Kanna learns something in Hiroshima about herself and the world and puts that message into her painting. I wanted to depict the whole process, right up to the point where viewers come to see her painting and receive that message.” Alexander Ludwig on ‘Unabomber’ Movie, His ‘Hunger Games’ Death Scene and ‘White Lotus’ Season 4: ‘It’s F—ing Wild’ Blackpink and ‘White Lotus’ Star Lisa Documentary ‘Always Lalisa’ Sets Global Release France Riots Put Hollywood Shoots on Alert as Curfews Disrupt Movie Theaters: It ‘Has Now Been Flagged as a Problem Area’ Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations Loading comments...

Former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly hosted the first-ever “ Bigg Boss Bangla,” which launched this quarter on streaming service JioHotstar . In sports, the England–India cricket series gave JioHotstar its biggest audience yet for a bilateral series played abroad.
